14.t: Working with data: transpiration over a day
q: Describe how the rate changes over the sunny day.
Almost zero at night, rising from about 06:00 to a peak at about 15:00 (4.4 g h⁻¹), then falling to a low level by 21:00.
Explain why the rate peaks in the early afternoon rather than at noon.
Air temperature is highest and humidity lowest in the early afternoon, so the water vapour gradient out of the stomata is steepest then.
Calculate the percentage decrease in the peak rate on the humid day.
Explain why the rate is lower on the humid day.
Humid air holds more water vapour, so the concentration gradient between the leaf air spaces and the outside air is smaller: slower diffusion out through the stomata.
Suggest why the rate is not zero at night.
Some stomata stay partly open, and some water is lost through the cuticle.

16.t: Working with data: a potometer experiment
q: Calculate the volume of water taken up per minute in still air. (Area of tube = 3.14 × r²)
Area = 3.14 × 0.5² = 0.785 mm². 20 × 0.785 = 15.7 mm³ in 5 min, so 3.1 mm³ min⁻¹.
Explain the result with the fan.
Moving air carries away the humid air next to the leaf, keeping the water vapour gradient steep, so water diffuses out faster.
Compare the two greasing results and explain the difference.
Greasing the lower surfaces almost stopped uptake (5 mm); greasing the upper surfaces barely changed it (19 mm). Most stomata are on the lower surface, and the grease blocks them.
Explain why a potometer measures water uptake, not exactly transpiration.
A little of the water taken up is used (in photosynthesis) or kept in the cells to keep them turgid, so uptake is not exactly equal to loss.
Suggest why the lamp was used with a heat filter.
To separate the effect of light (stomata opening) from the effect of temperature.
